assumptions.text: $N$ is a finite set of individuals, with no lower bound on their number.

statements.conclusion: Some SWF satisfies Par and IIA and is not dictatorial. As printed, this does not hold for a single individual, since then every SWF satisfying Par and IIA is dictatorial; the corrected statement, with at least two individuals, is part 2 of the main result above.

statements.title: Social choice functions, straightforwardness and procedure invariance
statements.statement:
1. A *social choice function* (SCF) $C$ assigns an alternative $C(\succ_1, \dots, \succ_n) \in X$ to every profile.
2. $C$ is *straightforward* if no individual ever gains by misrepresenting his preferences: for every profile, every individual $i$ and every report $\succ_i'$, it is not the case that $C(\succ_1, \dots, \succ_i', \dots, \succ_n) \succ_i C(\succ_1, \dots, \succ_i, \dots, \succ_n)$.
3. Let $Ch$ assign a choice function to every profile. $Ch$ satisfies *unanimity* if for every profile, every choice set $A$ and all ${x, y \in A}$: if ${y \succ_i x}$ for every $i$, then $x$ is not chosen from $A$.
4. $Ch$ is *invariant to the procedure* if, for every profile and every choice set $A$ split into two nonempty disjoint sets $A'$ and $A''$, choosing from $A'$ and from $A''$ and then choosing between the two picks gives the same outcome as choosing from $A$ directly.

assumptions.text: $X$ is a set of alternatives, and each individual in $N$ has an ordering of $X$.
Parts 3 and 4: $Ch$ assigns a choice function to every profile.

statements.title: Unanimity and procedure invariance force a dictatorship
statements.statement: As printed: Dutta, Jackson, and Le Breton (2001) show that only dictatorships satisfy both unanimity and invariance to the procedure, for a function $Ch$ that assigns a choice function to every profile. No condition is stated on the number of alternatives or on the domain of choice sets.

assumptions.text: $X$ is a set of alternatives, and each individual of a finite set $N$ has an ordering.
$Ch$ assigns a choice function to every profile.

statements.conclusion: $Ch$ is a dictatorship. As printed, this does not hold in full generality (see the counterexample).

statements.title: Unanimity and procedure invariance without a dictator
statements.statement:
Let ${X = \{0, 1\}}$, let $N$ have three individuals, and let the choice sets be all nonempty subsets of $X$. The rule that, from a set containing both alternatives, picks $1$ only when every individual strictly prefers $1$ to $0$, and $0$ otherwise, satisfies unanimity and invariance to the procedure; but no individual is a dictator, in the sense that the pick from every set is that individual’s best element of the set at every profile.

With two alternatives every choice function is path independent, so invariance to the procedure holds automatically, and unanimity alone already admits a rule with no dictator.
statements.conclusion: The printed statement does not hold with two alternatives and three individuals.

statements.title: Arrow’s theorem for choice rules (Dutta–Jackson–Le Breton)
statements.statement: Let $N$ be finite, let $X$ contain **at least three** alternatives, and let $Ch$ assign to every profile a choice function whose domain **contains every nonempty finite subset of** $X$. If $Ch$ satisfies unanimity, invariance to the procedure and **independence of infeasible alternatives** (whenever two profiles rank the alternatives of a choice set $A$ in the same way, the choice from $A$ is the same at both), then some individual $d$ is a dictator: at every profile, the choice from every set $A$ is $d$’s best element of $A$.

assumptions.text: $N$ is a finite set of individuals.
$Ch$ assigns a choice function to every profile.
Every nonempty finite subset of $X$ is an admissible choice set.

statements.conclusion: One individual’s ordering determines every choice.

statements.title: Every straightforward SCF is a dictatorship
statements.statement: As printed: the Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem states that any straightforward SCF is a dictatorship, i.e. a function that consistently picks the dictator’s most preferred alternatives. No condition is stated on the number of alternatives or on the range of the SCF.

assumptions.text: $X$ is a set of alternatives, with no condition.
$N$ is a finite set of individuals.
$C$ is a straightforward social choice function.

statements.conclusion: $C$ is a dictatorship. As printed, this does not hold in full generality (see the counterexample).

statements.title: A straightforward social choice function with no dictator
statements.statement: Let $X$ contain two distinct alternatives $a$ and $b$, and $N$ two distinct individuals. The SCF that picks $b$ when every individual strictly prefers $b$ to $a$, and $a$ otherwise, is straightforward, but there is no individual whose most preferred alternative it always picks, whether “most preferred” is taken among the alternatives the rule can select or among all of $X$. When “most preferred” means best in all of $X$, the printed statement does not hold for any number of individuals; and some SCF is not straightforward, so the hypothesis is not vacuous.
statements.conclusion: The printed statement does not hold for any such $X$ and $N$.

statements.title: Gibbard–Satterthwaite: strategy-proof onto SCFs are dictatorial
statements.statement: Let $N$ be finite and let $X$ contain **at least three** alternatives. If $C$ is a straightforward SCF that is **onto** $X$ (every alternative is chosen at some profile), then there is an individual $i$ such that at every profile $C$ picks $i$’s most preferred alternative in $X$.

assumptions.text: $N$ is a finite set of individuals.

statements.conclusion: $C$ is dictatorial: it always picks the top alternative of one fixed individual.

statements.title: Pareto and monotonicity force a dictatorship
statements.statement: As printed: consider a change in a profile so that an alternative $a$, which individual $i$ ranked below $b$, is now ranked by $i$ above $b$. Monotonicity requires that there is no alternative $c$ such that this change lowers the ranking of $a$ relative to $c$. Muller and Satterthwaite (1977)’s theorem shows that the only SWFs satisfying Par and monotonicity are dictatorships. No condition on the number of alternatives is stated.

assumptions.text: $X$ is a set of alternatives, with no condition on its size.
$N$ is a finite set of individuals.
$F$ is a social welfare function satisfying Par.

statements.conclusion: $F$ is dictatorial. As printed, this does not hold in full generality: it does not hold with two alternatives (see the counterexample).

statements.title: With two alternatives, majority rule is monotone and not dictatorial
statements.statement: Let $X$ have two alternatives and $N$ three individuals. The majority rule satisfies Par and monotonicity in its strongest reading (when individual $i$ moves $a$ above $b$, every strict or weak social preference for $a$ over any $c$ persists), and it is not dictatorial. The printed statement also does not hold under every weaker reading of the monotonicity gloss, under any condition implied by Par and IIA, and under any condition that the majority rule satisfies.
statements.conclusion: The printed statement does not hold with two alternatives and three individuals.

statements.title: Pareto and strong positive association force a dictatorship
statements.statement: Let $N$ be finite and let $X$ contain **at least three** alternatives. Every SWF $F$ that satisfies Par and **strong positive association** is dictatorial. Here $F$ satisfies strong positive association if, whenever profiles $P$ and $P'$ and an alternative $a$ are such that every alternative an individual ranks strictly below $a$ in $P$ is still ranked strictly below $a$ by that individual in $P'$, then for every $c$, a strict social preference for $a$ over $c$ at $P$ persists at $P'$, and so does a weak one.

assumptions.text: $N$ is a finite set of individuals.
$F$ satisfies strong positive association, in place of the informally glossed monotonicity.

statements.conclusion: $F$ is dictatorial.

statements.title: Indifference is symmetric
statements.statement: Let ${\succsim}$ be a complete, reflexive and transitive preference relation on a set ${X},$ with ${x\sim y}$ iff ${x\succsim y}$ and ${y\succsim x},$ and ${x\succ y}$ iff ${x\succsim y}$ and not ${y\succsim x}.$ If ${x\sim y},$ then ${y\sim x}.$

assumptions.text: ${\succsim}$ is complete: any two distinct alternatives are comparable.
${\succsim}$ is transitive: ${x\succsim y}$ and ${y\succsim z}$ imply ${x\succsim z}.$

statements.title: Indifference is reflexive
statements.statement: Let ${\succsim}$ be a complete, reflexive and transitive preference relation on a set ${X},$ with ${x\sim y}$ iff ${x\succsim y}$ and ${y\succsim x},$ and ${x\succ y}$ iff ${x\succsim y}$ and not ${y\succsim x}.$ Then ${x\sim x}$ for every ${x\in X}.$

assumptions.text: ${\succsim}$ is complete: any two distinct alternatives are comparable.
${\succsim}$ is transitive: ${x\succsim y}$ and ${y\succsim z}$ imply ${x\succsim z}.$

statements.title: Indifference is transitive
statements.statement: Let ${\succsim}$ be a complete, reflexive and transitive preference relation on a set ${X},$ with ${x\sim y}$ iff ${x\succsim y}$ and ${y\succsim x},$ and ${x\succ y}$ iff ${x\succsim y}$ and not ${y\succsim x}.$ If ${x\sim y}$ and ${y\sim z},$ then ${x\sim z}.$

assumptions.text: ${\succsim}$ is complete: any two distinct alternatives are comparable.
${\succsim}$ is transitive: ${x\succsim y}$ and ${y\succsim z}$ imply ${x\succsim z}.$

statements.title: Strict preference followed by weak preference is strict
statements.statement: Let ${\succsim}$ be a complete, reflexive and transitive preference relation on a set ${X},$ with ${x\sim y}$ iff ${x\succsim y}$ and ${y\succsim x},$ and ${x\succ y}$ iff ${x\succsim y}$ and not ${y\succsim x}.$ If ${x\succ y}$ and ${y\succsim z},$ then ${x\succ z}.$

assumptions.text: ${\succsim}$ is complete: any two distinct alternatives are comparable.
${\succsim}$ is transitive: ${x\succsim y}$ and ${y\succsim z}$ imply ${x\succsim z}.$

statements.title: Indifference is an equivalence relation
statements.statement: Let ${\succsim}$ be a complete, reflexive and transitive preference relation on a set ${X},$ with ${x\sim y}$ iff ${x\succsim y}$ and ${y\succsim x},$ and ${x\succ y}$ iff ${x\succsim y}$ and not ${y\succsim x}.$ Then ${\sim}$ is an equivalence relation: reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

assumptions.text: ${\succsim}$ is complete: any two distinct alternatives are comparable.
${\succsim}$ is transitive: ${x\succsim y}$ and ${y\succsim z}$ imply ${x\succsim z}.$

statements.title: Increasing transformations of a utility represent the same preference
statements.statement:
Let ${\succsim}$ be a binary relation on a set ${X},$ let ${u:X\to\mathbb{R}}$ represent it, ${x\succsim y\iff u(x)\ge u(y)},$ and let ${f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ be strictly increasing. Then ${v=f\circ u}$ also represents ${\succsim}$:
$$x\succsim y\iff f\big(u(x)\big)\ge f\big(u(y)\big).$$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ represents ${\succsim}$: ${x\succsim y}$ if and only if ${u(x)\ge u(y)}.$

entries.title: Lexicographic preferences have no utility representation

statements.title: Lexicographic preferences on the plane are a preference relation
statements.statement: On ${X=\mathbb{R}^2}$ let ${(x_1,x_2)\succsim(y_1,y_2)}$ if and only if ${x_1>y_1},$ or ${x_1=y_1}$ and ${x_2\ge y_2}.$ Then ${\succsim}$ is complete, reflexive and transitive.

statements.title: No utility function represents lexicographic preferences
statements.statement: On ${X=\mathbb{R}^2}$ let ${(x_1,x_2)\succsim(y_1,y_2)}$ if and only if ${x_1>y_1},$ or ${x_1=y_1}$ and ${x_2\ge y_2}.$ Then there is no function ${u:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}}$ with ${x\succsim y\iff u(x)\ge u(y)}$ for all ${x,y}.$

statements.title: Lexicographic preferences violate only continuity
statements.statement: On ${X=\mathbb{R}^2}$ let ${(x_1,x_2)\succsim(y_1,y_2)}$ if and only if ${x_1>y_1},$ or ${x_1=y_1}$ and ${x_2\ge y_2}.$ Then ${\succsim}$ is complete, reflexive, transitive and strictly monotone (${x\ge y}$ coordinatewise and ${x\neq y}$ imply ${x\succ y}$), but not continuous: it is not true that whenever ${a\succ b},$ every ${x}$ near ${a}$ and every ${y}$ near ${b}$ satisfy ${x\succ y}.$

statements.title: Survey answers and true preferences, a question for discussion
statements.statement: The question asks for a discussion of contingent valuation and of how to test survey answers against the axioms of rational preference. It contains no formal statement to check.

statements.title: Optimal coverage equates marginal benefit and marginal cost
statements.statement:
A consumer with a strictly concave von Neumann–Morgenstern utility ${u:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ and wealth ${w}$ loses ${L}$ with probability ${p\in[0,1]}.$ Coverage ${q\in\mathbb{R}}$ costs ${\pi q},$ so her final wealth is ${w-\pi q}$ without the loss and ${w-L+(1-\pi)q}$ with it, and her expected utility is
$$\begin{aligned}U(q)&=(1-p)\,u(w-\pi q)\\&\quad+p\,u\big(w-L+(1-\pi)q\big).\end{aligned}$$
Coverage ${q}$ is optimal if it maximizes ${U}$ over all real ${q}.$ Then ${q}$ is optimal if and only if ${u}$ has supporting slopes ${s_0}$ at ${w-\pi q}$ and ${s_1}$ at ${w-L+(1-\pi)q}$ (so that ${u(t)\le u(a)+s\,(t-a)}$ for all ${t}$ at the corresponding point ${a}$) with
$$p\,(1-\pi)\,s_1=\pi\,(1-p)\,s_0 .$$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is strictly concave: the consumer is strictly risk averse.

statements.title: With actuarially fair insurance, she insures fully
statements.statement:
A consumer with a strictly concave von Neumann–Morgenstern utility ${u:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ and wealth ${w}$ loses ${L}$ with probability ${p\in[0,1]}.$ Coverage ${q\in\mathbb{R}}$ costs ${\pi q},$ so her final wealth is ${w-\pi q}$ without the loss and ${w-L+(1-\pi)q}$ with it, and her expected utility is
$$\begin{aligned}U(q)&=(1-p)\,u(w-\pi q)\\&\quad+p\,u\big(w-L+(1-\pi)q\big).\end{aligned}$$
Coverage ${q}$ is optimal if it maximizes ${U}$ over all real ${q}.$ If insurance is actuarially fair, ${\pi=p},$ then ${q}$ is optimal if and only if ${q=L}$ or ${p\in\{0,1\}}.$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is strictly concave: the consumer is strictly risk averse.

statements.title: With loaded insurance, coverage is on one side of full
statements.statement:
A consumer with a strictly concave von Neumann–Morgenstern utility ${u:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ and wealth ${w}$ loses ${L}$ with probability ${p\in[0,1]}.$ Coverage ${q\in\mathbb{R}}$ costs ${\pi q},$ so her final wealth is ${w-\pi q}$ without the loss and ${w-L+(1-\pi)q}$ with it, and her expected utility is
$$\begin{aligned}U(q)&=(1-p)\,u(w-\pi q)\\&\quad+p\,u\big(w-L+(1-\pi)q\big).\end{aligned}$$
Coverage ${q}$ is optimal if it maximizes ${U}$ over all real ${q}.$ If ${\pi>p},$ then ${q}$ is optimal if and only if the marginal condition of part (a) holds and, writing ${\bar w=w-\pi L}$ for the wealth full coverage guarantees:

- if ${u}$ is higher at some wealth above ${\bar w},$ then ${q\le L};$
- if ${\bar w}$ maximizes ${u},$ then ${q=L};$
- if ${u}$ is higher at some wealth below ${\bar w},$ then ${q\ge L}.$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is strictly concave: the consumer is strictly risk averse.

entries.title: To feed the parking meter or not

statements.title: The elasticity of the gain from paying with respect to detection
statements.statement:
Let ${u:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ be infinitely differentiable, strictly increasing and concave. A citizen with wealth ${w}$ who feeds the meter pays ${m};$ one who parks illegally is fined ${f}$ with probability ${p\in[0,1]}.$ The gain from feeding the meter is
$$\begin{gathered}\Delta(w)=u(w-m)\\-\big[p\,u(w-f)+(1-p)\,u(w)\big].\end{gathered}$$ Then the elasticity of ${\Delta}$ with respect to ${p}$ is
$$\begin{aligned}\varepsilon_p&=\frac{p}{\Delta}\,\frac{\partial\Delta}{\partial p}\\[4pt]&=\frac{p\,\big[u(w)-u(w-f)\big]}{\Delta}.\end{aligned}$$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is differentiable as many times as needed.

statements.title: The elasticity of the gain from paying with respect to the fine
statements.statement:
Let ${u:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ be infinitely differentiable, strictly increasing and concave. A citizen with wealth ${w}$ who feeds the meter pays ${m};$ one who parks illegally is fined ${f}$ with probability ${p\in[0,1]}.$ The gain from feeding the meter is
$$\begin{gathered}\Delta(w)=u(w-m)\\-\big[p\,u(w-f)+(1-p)\,u(w)\big].\end{gathered}$$ Then the elasticity of ${\Delta}$ with respect to ${f}$ is
$$\begin{aligned}\varepsilon_f&=\frac{f}{\Delta}\,\frac{\partial\Delta}{\partial f}\\[4pt]&=\frac{p\,f\,u'(w-f)}{\Delta}.\end{aligned}$$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is differentiable as many times as needed.

statements.title: Payers respond weakly more to fines, violators weakly more to detection
statements.statement:
Let ${u:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ be infinitely differentiable, strictly increasing and concave. A citizen with wealth ${w}$ who feeds the meter pays ${m};$ one who parks illegally is fined ${f}$ with probability ${p\in[0,1]}.$ The gain from feeding the meter is
$$\begin{gathered}\Delta(w)=u(w-m)\\-\big[p\,u(w-f)+(1-p)\,u(w)\big].\end{gathered}$$ Then the elasticities of the previous two parts satisfy
$$\begin{aligned}\Delta>0\ &\Longrightarrow\ \varepsilon_p\le\varepsilon_f,\\ \Delta<0\ &\Longrightarrow\ \varepsilon_f\le\varepsilon_p.\end{aligned}$$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is differentiable as many times as needed.

statements.title: A wealth threshold separates payers from violators
statements.statement:
Let ${u:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ be infinitely differentiable, strictly increasing and concave. A citizen with wealth ${w}$ who feeds the meter pays ${m};$ one who parks illegally is fined ${f}$ with probability ${p\in[0,1]}.$ The gain from feeding the meter is
$$\begin{gathered}\Delta(w)=u(w-m)\\-\big[p\,u(w-f)+(1-p)\,u(w)\big].\end{gathered}$$ Citizens’ wealth ranges over ${[\underline w,\bar w]};$ a citizen feeds the meter when ${\Delta>0}$ and parks illegally otherwise. If ${\Delta}$ is decreasing in wealth on that range and both groups are present, there is exactly one ${w^*\in[\underline w,\bar w]}$ such that ${\Delta(w)>0}$ for every ${w<w^*}$ and ${\Delta(w)\le 0}$ for every ${w>w^*}$ in the range.

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is differentiable as many times as needed.
${\Delta}$ is decreasing in wealth on ${[\underline w,\bar w]}.$
Some citizen in the range feeds the meter: ${\Delta(w)>0}.$
Some citizen in the range parks illegally: ${\Delta(w)\le 0}.$

statements.title: Both groups present forces m > pf
statements.statement:

$$\begin{gathered}\Delta(w)=u(w-m)\\-\big[p\,u(w-f)+(1-p)\,u(w)\big].\end{gathered}$$ Citizens’ wealth ranges over ${[\underline w,\bar w]};$ a citizen feeds the meter when ${\Delta>0}$ and parks illegally otherwise. As printed: if ${\Delta}$ is decreasing in wealth on that range and both groups are present, then ${pf<m}.$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is differentiable as many times as needed.
${\Delta}$ is decreasing in wealth on ${[\underline w,\bar w]}.$
Some citizen in the range feeds the meter: ${\Delta(w)>0}.$
Some citizen in the range parks illegally: ${\Delta(w)\le 0}.$

statements.title: With strictly concave utility, both groups present forces m > pf
statements.statement:
Let ${u:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ be infinitely differentiable, strictly increasing and concave. A citizen with wealth ${w}$ who feeds the meter pays ${m};$ one who parks illegally is fined ${f}$ with probability ${p\in[0,1]}.$ The gain from feeding the meter is
$$\begin{gathered}\Delta(w)=u(w-m)\\-\big[p\,u(w-f)+(1-p)\,u(w)\big].\end{gathered}$$ Citizens’ wealth ranges over ${[\underline w,\bar w]};$ a citizen feeds the meter when ${\Delta>0}$ and parks illegally otherwise. If ${u}$ is strictly concave, ${\Delta}$ is decreasing in wealth on that range and both groups are present, then ${pf<m}.$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is differentiable as many times as needed.
${\Delta}$ is decreasing in wealth on ${[\underline w,\bar w]}.$
Some citizen in the range feeds the meter: ${\Delta(w)>0}.$
Some citizen in the range parks illegally: ${\Delta(w)\le 0}.$

statements.title: If violators strictly prefer to park, both groups force m > pf
statements.statement:
Let ${u:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ be infinitely differentiable, strictly increasing and concave. A citizen with wealth ${w}$ who feeds the meter pays ${m};$ one who parks illegally is fined ${f}$ with probability ${p\in[0,1]}.$ The gain from feeding the meter is
$$\begin{gathered}\Delta(w)=u(w-m)\\-\big[p\,u(w-f)+(1-p)\,u(w)\big].\end{gathered}$$ Citizens’ wealth ranges over ${[\underline w,\bar w]}.$ If ${\Delta}$ is decreasing in wealth on that range, some citizen has ${\Delta>0}$ and some citizen has ${\Delta<0},$ then ${pf<m}.$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is differentiable as many times as needed.
${\Delta}$ is decreasing in wealth on ${[\underline w,\bar w]}.$
Some citizen in the range feeds the meter: ${\Delta(w)>0}.$
Some citizen in the range strictly prefers to park illegally: ${\Delta(w)<0}.$

statements.title: A higher fine never shrinks the set of meter-feeders
statements.statement:
Let ${u:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ be infinitely differentiable, strictly increasing and concave. A citizen with wealth ${w}$ who feeds the meter pays ${m};$ one who parks illegally is fined ${f}$ with probability ${p\in[0,1]}.$ The gain from feeding the meter is
$$\begin{gathered}\Delta(w)=u(w-m)\\-\big[p\,u(w-f)+(1-p)\,u(w)\big].\end{gathered}$$ Let ${F(f,m,p)}$ be the set of wealth levels ${w\in[\underline w,\bar w]}$ with ${\Delta(w)>0}$: the citizens who feed the meter. Then ${F}$ is weakly increasing in ${f}$: ${f\le f'}$ implies ${F(f,m,p)\subseteq F(f',m,p)}.$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is differentiable as many times as needed.

statements.title: A pricier meter never enlarges the set of meter-feeders
statements.statement:
Let ${u:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ be infinitely differentiable, strictly increasing and concave. A citizen with wealth ${w}$ who feeds the meter pays ${m};$ one who parks illegally is fined ${f}$ with probability ${p\in[0,1]}.$ The gain from feeding the meter is
$$\begin{gathered}\Delta(w)=u(w-m)\\-\big[p\,u(w-f)+(1-p)\,u(w)\big].\end{gathered}$$ Let ${F(f,m,p)}$ be the set of wealth levels ${w\in[\underline w,\bar w]}$ with ${\Delta(w)>0}$: the citizens who feed the meter. Then ${F}$ is weakly decreasing in ${m}$: ${m\le m'}$ implies ${F(f,m',p)\subseteq F(f,m,p)}.$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is differentiable as many times as needed.

statements.title: With a nonnegative fine, more policing never shrinks the set of payers
statements.statement:
Let ${u:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ be infinitely differentiable, strictly increasing and concave. A citizen with wealth ${w}$ who feeds the meter pays ${m};$ one who parks illegally is fined ${f}$ with probability ${p\in[0,1]}.$ The gain from feeding the meter is
$$\begin{gathered}\Delta(w)=u(w-m)\\-\big[p\,u(w-f)+(1-p)\,u(w)\big].\end{gathered}$$ Let ${F(f,m,p)}$ be the set of wealth levels ${w\in[\underline w,\bar w]}$ with ${\Delta(w)>0}$: the citizens who feed the meter. Then, as ${p}$ ranges over ${[0,1]}$: if ${f\ge 0},$ ${F}$ is weakly increasing in ${p};$ if ${f\le 0},$ it is weakly decreasing in ${p}.$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is differentiable as many times as needed.

entries.title: Should the young hold more stocks?

statements.title: Age and the share of wealth in stocks, a question for discussion
statements.statement: The question asks for a discussion of why younger investors might hold a larger share of their wealth in stocks. It contains no formal statement to check.

entries.title: Quasi-linear preferences have no wealth effects

statements.title: Demand for goods 2 to n does not depend on wealth
statements.statement:
The consumption set is ${X=\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-1}_+}$ with ${n\ge 1}$ goods: any real amount of the first good, and nonnegative amounts of the others. A preference ${\succsim}$ on ${X}$ is *strictly convex* if ${a\succsim y},$ ${b\succsim y}$ and ${a\neq b}$ imply that every strict mixture of ${a}$ and ${b}$ is strictly better than ${y},$ and *quasi-linear in the first good* if ${x\succsim y}$ implies $x+\varepsilon e_1\succsim y+\varepsilon e_1$ for every real ${\varepsilon}.$ Prices are normalized so that ${p_1=1},$ and a bundle is demanded at ${(p,w)}$ if it is affordable, ${p\cdot x\le w},$ and at least as good as every affordable bundle. If ${x}$ is demanded at ${(p,w)}$ and ${x'}$ at ${(p,w')},$ then, for every good ${k=2,\dots,n},$
$$x_k=x'_k.$$

assumptions.text: ${\succsim}$ is quasi-linear in the first good.

statements.title: Hicksian demand for goods 2 to n does not depend on the target utility
statements.statement:
The consumption set is ${X=\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-1}_+}$ with ${n\ge 1}$ goods: any real amount of the first good, and nonnegative amounts of the others. A preference ${\succsim}$ on ${X}$ is *strictly convex* if ${a\succsim y},$ ${b\succsim y}$ and ${a\neq b}$ imply that every strict mixture of ${a}$ and ${b}$ is strictly better than ${y},$ and *quasi-linear in the first good* if ${x\succsim y}$ implies $x+\varepsilon e_1\succsim y+\varepsilon e_1$ for every real ${\varepsilon}.$ Prices are normalized so that ${p_1=1},$ and a bundle is demanded at ${(p,w)}$ if it is affordable, ${p\cdot x\le w},$ and at least as good as every affordable bundle. Let ${u}$ represent ${\succsim}.$ A bundle ${h}$ is a Hicksian demand at ${(p,\bar u)}$ if ${u(h)\ge\bar u}$ and ${p\cdot h\le p\cdot y}$ for every ${y}$ with ${u(y)\ge\bar u}.$ If ${h}$ is a Hicksian demand at ${(p,\bar u)}$ and ${h'}$ at ${(p,\bar u')},$ then, for every good ${k=2,\dots,n},$
$$h_k=h'_k.$$

assumptions.text: ${\succsim}$ is quasi-linear in the first good.
${u}$ represents ${\succsim}$: ${x\succsim y}$ if and only if ${u(x)\ge u(y)}.$
${h}$ is a Hicksian demand at ${(p,\bar u)}$ and ${h'}$ at ${(p,\bar u')}.$

statements.title: Indirect utility takes the form v(p, w) = w + φ(p)
statements.statement:
The consumption set is ${X=\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-1}_+}$ with ${n\ge 1}$ goods: any real amount of the first good, and nonnegative amounts of the others. A preference ${\succsim}$ on ${X}$ is *strictly convex* if ${a\succsim y},$ ${b\succsim y}$ and ${a\neq b}$ imply that every strict mixture of ${a}$ and ${b}$ is strictly better than ${y},$ and *quasi-linear in the first good* if ${x\succsim y}$ implies $x+\varepsilon e_1\succsim y+\varepsilon e_1$ for every real ${\varepsilon}.$ Prices are normalized so that ${p_1=1},$ and a bundle is demanded at ${(p,w)}$ if it is affordable, ${p\cdot x\le w},$ and at least as good as every affordable bundle. Let ${u}$ represent ${\succsim}.$ A function ${v(p,w)}$ is an indirect utility function on normalized prices if, whenever ${x}$ is demanded at ${(p,w)}$ and ${x'}$ at ${(p',w')}$ with ${p_1=p'_1=1},$ ${x\succsim x'}$ holds exactly when ${v(p,w)\ge v(p',w')}.$ Then for some function ${\varphi}$ of prices,
$$v(p,w)=w+\varphi(p)$$
is an indirect utility function on normalized prices.

assumptions.text: ${\succsim}$ is quasi-linear in the first good.
${u}$ represents ${\succsim}$: ${x\succsim y}$ if and only if ${u(x)\ge u(y)}.$

statements.title: The expenditure function takes the form e(p, ū) = c(ū) − φ(p)
statements.statement:
The consumption set is ${X=\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-1}_+}$ with ${n\ge 1}$ goods: any real amount of the first good, and nonnegative amounts of the others. A preference ${\succsim}$ on ${X}$ is *strictly convex* if ${a\succsim y},$ ${b\succsim y}$ and ${a\neq b}$ imply that every strict mixture of ${a}$ and ${b}$ is strictly better than ${y},$ and *quasi-linear in the first good* if ${x\succsim y}$ implies $x+\varepsilon e_1\succsim y+\varepsilon e_1$ for every real ${\varepsilon}.$ Prices are normalized so that ${p_1=1},$ and a bundle is demanded at ${(p,w)}$ if it is affordable, ${p\cdot x\le w},$ and at least as good as every affordable bundle. Let ${u}$ represent ${\succsim}.$ A bundle ${h}$ is a Hicksian demand at ${(p,\bar u)}$ if ${u(h)\ge\bar u}$ and ${p\cdot h\le p\cdot y}$ for every ${y}$ with ${u(y)\ge\bar u}.$ Call ${e}$ an expenditure at ${(p,\bar u)}$ if ${e=p\cdot h}$ for some Hicksian demand ${h}$ at ${(p,\bar u)}.$ A function ${v(p,w)}$ is an indirect utility function on normalized prices if, whenever ${x}$ is demanded at ${(p,w)}$ and ${x'}$ at ${(p',w')}$ with ${p_1=p'_1=1},$ ${x\succsim x'}$ holds exactly when ${v(p,w)\ge v(p',w')}.$ Then there are functions ${c}$ of the target utility and ${\varphi}$ of prices such that ${w+\varphi(p)}$ is an indirect utility function on normalized prices and, for every ${p}$ with ${p_1=1},$ every expenditure at ${(p,\bar u)}$ is
$$e(p,\bar u)=c(\bar u)-\varphi(p).$$

entries.title: Demand for the utility max{ax, ay} + min{x, y}

statements.title: Indifference curves are kinked on the diagonal
statements.statement:
Let ${0<a<1}$ and $u(x,y)=\max\{ax,ay\}+\min\{x,y\}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}.$ Let ${\succsim}$ be the preference that ${u}$ represents. A bundle ${z}$ is indifferent to ${b}$ if and only if ${z}$ lies on the indifference curve at level ${c=u(b)}$:
$$\begin{gathered}\{z:\ z_2\le z_1,\ az_1+z_2=c\}\\ \cup\ \{z:\ z_1\le z_2,\ z_1+az_2=c\}.\end{gathered}$$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ represents ${\succsim}$: ${s\succsim t}$ if and only if ${u(s)\ge u(t)}.$

statements.title: Marshallian demand: a corner, the kink, or a segment
statements.statement:
Let ${0<a<1}$ and $u(x,y)=\max\{ax,ay\}+\min\{x,y\}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}.$ Let ${p\gg 0}$ and let ${w}$ be any wealth level. A bundle ${x}$ is in the Marshallian demand at ${(p,w)}$ if and only if:

- ${p_2<ap_1}$: ${x=(0,\,w/p_2)};$
- ${p_2=ap_1}$: ${p\cdot x=w}$ and ${x_1\le x_2};$
- ${ap_1<p_2}$ and ${ap_2<p_1}$: ${x_1=x_2=w/(p_1+p_2)};$
- ${p_1=ap_2}$: ${p\cdot x=w}$ and ${x_2\le x_1};$
- ${p_1<ap_2}$: ${x=(w/p_1,\,0)}.$

statements.title: Hicksian demand: a corner, the kink, or a segment
statements.statement:
Let ${0<a<1}$ and $u(x,y)=\max\{ax,ay\}+\min\{x,y\}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}.$ Let ${p\gg 0}$ and let the target ${\bar u}$ be at least ${u(0,0)=0}.$ A bundle ${h}$ is in the Hicksian demand, that is ${u(h)\ge\bar u}$ and ${p\cdot h\le p\cdot y}$ for every ${y}$ with ${u(y)\ge\bar u},$ if and only if:

- ${p_2<ap_1}$: ${h=(0,\,\bar u/a)};$
- ${p_2=ap_1}$: ${h_1+ah_2=\bar u}$ and ${h_1\le h_2};$
- ${ap_1<p_2}$ and ${ap_2<p_1}$: ${h_1=h_2=\bar u/(1+a)};$
- ${p_1=ap_2}$: ${ah_1+h_2=\bar u}$ and ${h_2\le h_1};$
- ${p_1<ap_2}$: ${h=(\bar u/a,\,0)}.$

assumptions.text: the target is at least the utility of the zero bundle: ${\bar u\ge u(0,0)=0}.$

statements.statement:

statements.title: Every good has at least one substitute
statements.statement: For a utility function ${u}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^L_+},$ the Hicksian demand ${h(p,\bar u)}$ consists of the bundles of least cost ${p\cdot x}$ among those with ${u(x)\ge\bar u}.$ Goods ${i}$ and ${j}$ are *substitutes* at ${(p,\bar u)}$ if, for good-${j}$ prices near ${p_j}$ with the other prices fixed, the Hicksian demand is a single bundle whose ${i}$-th coordinate has a derivative ${\partial h_i/\partial p_j\ge0}$ at ${p_j}.$ As printed: for every utility function ${u},$ price vector ${p},$ level ${\bar u}$ and good ${i},$ there is a good ${j\neq i}$ such that ${i}$ and ${j}$ are substitutes at ${(p,\bar u)}.$

statements.statement: For a utility function ${u}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^L_+},$ the Hicksian demand ${h(p,\bar u)}$ consists of the bundles of least cost ${p\cdot x}$ among those with ${u(x)\ge\bar u}.$ Goods ${i}$ and ${j}$ are *substitutes* at ${(p,\bar u)}$ if, for good-${j}$ prices near ${p_j}$ with the other prices fixed, the Hicksian demand is a single bundle whose ${i}$-th coordinate has a derivative ${\partial h_i/\partial p_j\ge0}$ at ${p_j}.$ It is not the case that, for every utility function, price vector ${p},$ level ${\bar u}$ and goods ${i,j},$ whenever ${i}$ and ${j}$ are substitutes at ${(p,\bar u)},$ so are ${j}$ and ${i}.$

statements.statement: For a utility function ${u}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^L_+},$ the Hicksian demand ${h(p,\bar u)}$ consists of the bundles of least cost ${p\cdot x}$ among those with ${u(x)\ge\bar u}.$ Goods ${i}$ and ${j}$ are *substitutes* at ${(p,\bar u)}$ if, for good-${j}$ prices near ${p_j}$ with the other prices fixed, the Hicksian demand is a single bundle whose ${i}$-th coordinate has a derivative ${\partial h_i/\partial p_j\ge0}$ at ${p_j}.$ There are a utility function, a level ${\bar u},$ two goods ${i\neq j}$ and two price vectors ${p\neq p'}$ such that ${i}$ and ${j}$ are substitutes at ${(p,\bar u)},$ while at ${p'}$ the Hicksian demand is a single bundle for good-${j}$ prices near ${p'_j}$ and ${\partial h_i/\partial p_j<0}$ at ${p'_j}.$

statements.title: Coffee can raise the payment to keep tea, at a fixed utility
statements.statement: For a utility function ${u}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^L_+},$ the Hicksian demand ${h(p,\bar u)}$ consists of the bundles of least cost ${p\cdot x}$ among those with ${u(x)\ge\bar u}.$ Goods ${i}$ and ${j}$ are *substitutes* at ${(p,\bar u)}$ if, for good-${j}$ prices near ${p_j}$ with the other prices fixed, the Hicksian demand is a single bundle whose ${i}$-th coordinate has a derivative ${\partial h_i/\partial p_j\ge0}$ at ${p_j}.$ Let coffee ${c}$ and tea ${t}$ be distinct goods. On our reading at a utility level, the amount paid at prices ${p}$ and level ${\bar u}$ to avoid losing tea is ${W=e'-e},$ where ${e}$ is the least cost of reaching ${\bar u}$ with the goods available and ${e'}$ the least cost of reaching it without tea. Let ${W_1}$ be this amount with coffee available and ${W_0}$ the amount with coffee unavailable. It is not true that ${W_1\le W_0}$ for every utility function, every two such goods that are substitutes at every price vector ${q\gg0}$ and every level, and all prices ${p}$ and levels ${\bar u}.$

statements.title: The expenditure function is e(p, ū) = ū√(p₁p₂)
statements.statement:
Let ${u}$ be a utility function on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ with indirect utility ${v(p,I)=I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}$: at all prices ${p\gg0}$ and income ${I>0},$ the greatest utility on the budget set is ${I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}.$ Let ${p\gg0}$ and ${\bar u>u(0)}.$ A number ${E}$ is the least cost of a bundle with utility at least ${\bar u}$ if and only if ${\bar u>0}$ and
$$E=\bar u\sqrt{p_1p_2}.$$

the target exceeds the utility of the zero bundle: ${\bar u>u(0)}.$

statements.title: The Hicksian demand splits spending equally
statements.statement:
Let ${u}$ be a utility function on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ with indirect utility ${v(p,I)=I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}$: at all prices ${p\gg0}$ and income ${I>0},$ the greatest utility on the budget set is ${I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}.$ Let ${p\gg0}$ and ${\bar u>u(0)}.$ A bundle ${h}$ has utility at least ${\bar u}$ and least cost among such bundles if and only if ${\bar u>0}$ and
$$h=\left(\frac{\bar u}{2}\sqrt{\frac{p_2}{p_1}},\ \frac{\bar u}{2}\sqrt{\frac{p_1}{p_2}}\right).$$

statements.title: A fourfold rise in p₁ has compensating variation −400
statements.statement:
Let ${u}$ be a utility function on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ with indirect utility ${v(p,I)=I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}$: at all prices ${p\gg0}$ and income ${I>0},$ the greatest utility on the budget set is ${I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}.$ The price of good 1 rises from ${100}$ to ${400},$ the price of good 2 stays at ${100},$ and income is ${I=400}.$ Let ${u^0}$ be the greatest utility at the initial prices, and let the compensating variation be ${CV=400-E},$ where ${E}$ is the least cost at the new prices of reaching ${u^0}.$ Then ${u^0}$ and ${E}$ exist, and a number ${c}$ is the compensating variation if and only if
$$c=-400.$$

assumptions.text: The indirect utility is ${v(p,I)=I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}$ at all prices ${p\gg0}$ and income ${I>0}.$

statements.title: Laspeyres index 5/2, Paasche index 8/5
statements.statement:
Let ${u}$ be a utility function on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ with indirect utility ${v(p,I)=I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}$: at all prices ${p\gg0}$ and income ${I>0},$ the greatest utility on the budget set is ${I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}.$ The price of good 1 rises from ${100}$ to ${400},$ the price of good 2 stays at ${100},$ and income is ${I=400}.$ The Laspeyres index is the cost at the new prices over the cost at the old prices of the bundle demanded before the change; the Paasche index is the same ratio for the bundle demanded after it. Numbers ${l}$ and ${q}$ are the Laspeyres and Paasche indexes if and only if
$$l=\frac{5}{2}\quad\text{and}\quad q=\frac{8}{5}.$$

assumptions.text: The indirect utility is ${v(p,I)=I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}$ at all prices ${p\gg0}$ and income ${I>0}.$

statements.title: Paasche < cost-of-living adjustment < Laspeyres
statements.statement:
Let ${u}$ be a utility function on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ with indirect utility ${v(p,I)=I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}$: at all prices ${p\gg0}$ and income ${I>0},$ the greatest utility on the budget set is ${I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}.$ The price of good 1 rises from ${100}$ to ${400},$ the price of good 2 stays at ${100},$ and income is ${I=400}.$ Let the cost-of-living adjustment suggested by the compensating variation ${c}$ be ${a=(400-c)/400}.$ Then every Laspeyres index ${l},$ every Paasche index ${q}$ and every such adjustment ${a}$ satisfy
$$q<a<l.$$

assumptions.text: The indirect utility is ${v(p,I)=I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}$ at all prices ${p\gg0}$ and income ${I>0}.$

entries.title: A monopolist’s output never rises with marginal cost

statements.title: Monopoly output is weakly decreasing in the unit cost
statements.statement:
Let the demand curve be any set ${D}$ of price–quantity points ${(p,x)},$ and let ${q(c)}$ be an output chosen at each unit cost ${c}.$ Consider the costs ${c}$ at which ${q(c)}$ is the quantity of a point of ${D}$ that maximizes profit ${px-cx}$ over ${D}.$ On those costs ${q}$ is weakly decreasing:
$$c<c'\ \Longrightarrow\ q(c)\ge q(c').$$

statements.title: A monotone change of variable preserves increasing differences
statements.statement:
A function ${f(x,y)}$ has *increasing differences* if, for all ${x\le x'},$ the difference ${f(x',y)-f(x,y)}$ is non-decreasing in ${y}.$ Let ${g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ be non-decreasing and let ${f:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}}$ have increasing differences. Then ${h(x,y)=f(g(x),y)}$ has increasing differences: for all ${x\le x'},$ the difference
$$f\big(g(x'),y\big)-f\big(g(x),y\big)$$
is non-decreasing in ${y}.$

statements.title: h(x − θ) has increasing differences exactly when h is concave
statements.statement: A function ${f(x,y)}$ has *increasing differences* if, for all ${x\le x'},$ the difference ${f(x',y)-f(x,y)}$ is non-decreasing in ${y}.$ Let ${h:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ be twice differentiable. Then ${f(x,\theta)=h(x-\theta)}$ has increasing differences if and only if ${h}$ is concave.

assumptions.text: ${h}$ is twice differentiable: ${h}$ and ${h'}$ are differentiable.

entries.title: Pricing against a shifting demand curve

statements.title: Concave demand makes the profit function concave
statements.statement: Let ${P}$ be an open interval of prices and ${Q(p,\theta)}$ a demand curve that, for every ${\theta},$ is non-increasing, differentiable and strictly positive in ${p}$ on ${P}.$ The firm chooses ${p\in P}$ to maximize the profit ${(p-c)\,Q(p,\theta)}$ for a constant unit cost ${c}.$ As printed: concave demand is sufficient to ensure that the profit function is concave. Nothing is said about how ${c}$ relates to the prices in ${P}.$

assumptions.text: The region of prices ${P}$ is an open interval.
Demand slopes downward: ${Q(\cdot,\theta)}$ is non-increasing on ${P}$ for every ${\theta}.$

statements.title: With price at least cost, concave demand makes profit concave
statements.statement: Let ${P}$ be an open interval of prices and ${Q(p,\theta)}$ a demand curve that, for every ${\theta},$ is non-increasing, differentiable and strictly positive in ${p}$ on ${P}.$ The firm chooses ${p\in P}$ to maximize the profit ${(p-c)\,Q(p,\theta)}$ for a constant unit cost ${c}.$ If ${c\le p}$ for every ${p\in P},$ then for every ${\theta}$: whenever ${Q(\cdot,\theta)}$ is concave on ${P},$ so is the profit ${p\mapsto(p-c)\,Q(p,\theta)}.$

assumptions.text: The region of prices ${P}$ is an open interval.
Demand slopes downward: ${Q(\cdot,\theta)}$ is non-increasing on ${P}$ for every ${\theta}.$
the unit cost is at most every price in the region: ${c\le p}$ for all ${p\in P}.$

statements.title: Demand grows more inelastic iff log Q has increasing differences
statements.statement: Let ${P}$ be an open interval of prices and ${Q(p,\theta)}$ a demand curve that, for every ${\theta},$ is non-increasing, differentiable and strictly positive in ${p}$ on ${P}.$ Let $\varepsilon(p,\theta)=p\,Q_p(p,\theta)/Q(p,\theta)$ be the price elasticity. ${\log Q}$ has *increasing differences* if, for all ${p\le p'}$ in ${P},$ ${\log Q(p',\theta)-\log Q(p,\theta)}$ is non-decreasing in ${\theta}.$ Then ${|\varepsilon(p,\theta)|}$ is non-increasing in ${\theta}$ at every ${p\in P}$ if and only if ${\log Q}$ has increasing differences.

assumptions.text: The region of prices ${P}$ is an open interval.
Demand slopes downward: ${Q(\cdot,\theta)}$ is non-increasing on ${P}$ for every ${\theta}.$

statements.title: Increasing differences of log Q make the price rise with θ
statements.statement: Let ${P}$ be an open interval of prices and ${Q(p,\theta)}$ a demand curve that, for every ${\theta},$ is non-increasing, differentiable and strictly positive in ${p}$ on ${P}.$ The firm chooses ${p\in P}$ to maximize the profit ${(p-c)\,Q(p,\theta)}$ for a constant unit cost ${c}.$ ${\log Q}$ has *increasing differences* if, for all ${p\le p'}$ in ${P},$ ${\log Q(p',\theta)-\log Q(p,\theta)}$ is non-decreasing in ${\theta}.$ If ${\log Q}$ has increasing differences then, for all ${\theta\le\theta'},$ the largest optimal price at ${\theta}$ is at most the largest optimal price at ${\theta'},$ whenever both exist. Moreover, ${\log Q}$ has increasing differences if and only if the absolute price elasticity ${|\varepsilon(p,\theta)|=|p\,Q_p(p,\theta)/Q(p,\theta)|}$ is non-increasing in ${\theta}$ at every ${p\in P}.$

assumptions.text: The region of prices ${P}$ is an open interval.
Demand slopes downward: ${Q(\cdot,\theta)}$ is non-increasing on ${P}$ for every ${\theta}.$

statements.title: Concave demand is not necessary for the prediction: first reading
statements.statement: Let ${P}$ be an open interval of prices and ${Q(p,\theta)}$ a demand curve that, for every ${\theta},$ is non-increasing, differentiable and strictly positive in ${p}$ on ${P}.$ The firm chooses ${p\in P}$ to maximize the profit ${(p-c)\,Q(p,\theta)}$ for a constant unit cost ${c}.$ ${\log Q}$ has *increasing differences* if, for all ${p\le p'}$ in ${P},$ ${\log Q(p',\theta)-\log Q(p,\theta)}$ is non-decreasing in ${\theta}.$ On our first reading of “necessary”: there is no demand curve, region ${P}$ and cost ${c}$ with these properties, with ${\log Q}$ having increasing differences and ${Q(\cdot,\theta)}$ not concave for some ${\theta},$ for which it fails that for all ${\theta\le\theta'},$ the largest optimal price at ${\theta}$ is at most the largest optimal price at ${\theta'},$ whenever both exist.

statements.title: Concave demand is not necessary for the prediction: second reading
statements.statement: Let ${P}$ be an open interval of prices and ${Q(p,\theta)}$ a demand curve that, for every ${\theta},$ is non-increasing, differentiable and strictly positive in ${p}$ on ${P}.$ The firm chooses ${p\in P}$ to maximize the profit ${(p-c)\,Q(p,\theta)}$ for a constant unit cost ${c}.$ On our second reading of “necessary”: it is not the case that every such demand curve and cost ${c}$ for which for all ${\theta\le\theta'},$ the largest optimal price at ${\theta}$ is at most the largest optimal price at ${\theta'},$ whenever both exist has ${Q(\cdot,\theta)}$ concave on ${P}$ at every ${\theta}.$

entries.title: Skill and the choice of technology

statements.title: Increasing differences make computer users buy more skill
statements.statement:
Let ${G}$ and ${H}$ be the production functions of the computer and the old-fashioned technology, and ${c}$ the total cost of skill, all functions of the skill level ${s}.$ The pair has *increasing differences in skill* if, whenever ${s\le s'},$
$$H(s')-H(s)\le G(s')-G(s),$$
that is, if ${G-H}$ is non-decreasing.
If ${G}$ and ${H}$ have increasing differences in skill then, for every cost of skill ${c}$ and every set ${S}$ of available skill levels, the largest maximizer of ${H(s)-c(s)}$ on ${S}$ is at most the largest maximizer of ${G(s)-c(s)}$ on ${S},$ whenever both exist.

statements.title: No weaker condition works for every cost of skill: first reading
statements.statement:
Let ${G}$ and ${H}$ be the production functions of the computer and the old-fashioned technology, and ${c}$ the total cost of skill, all functions of the skill level ${s}.$ The pair has *increasing differences in skill* if, whenever ${s\le s'},$
$$H(s')-H(s)\le G(s')-G(s),$$
that is, if ${G-H}$ is non-decreasing. Call a condition on pairs ${(G,H)}$ *sufficient* if, for every pair meeting it, every cost of skill ${c}$ and every set ${S}$ of available skill levels, the largest maximizer of ${H-c}$ on ${S}$ is at most the largest maximizer of ${G-c}$ on ${S},$ whenever both exist. On our first reading of “weaker”: no sufficient condition is implied by increasing differences and also holds at some pair without increasing differences.

statements.title: No weaker condition works for every cost of skill: second reading
statements.statement:
Let ${G}$ and ${H}$ be the production functions of the computer and the old-fashioned technology, and ${c}$ the total cost of skill, all functions of the skill level ${s}.$ The pair has *increasing differences in skill* if, whenever ${s\le s'},$
$$H(s')-H(s)\le G(s')-G(s),$$
that is, if ${G-H}$ is non-decreasing. Call a condition on pairs ${(G,H)}$ *sufficient* if, for every pair meeting it, every cost of skill ${c}$ and every set ${S}$ of available skill levels, the largest maximizer of ${H-c}$ on ${S}$ is at most the largest maximizer of ${G-c}$ on ${S},$ whenever both exist. On our second reading of “weaker”: no sufficient condition holds at a pair without increasing differences. Equivalently, every sufficient condition implies increasing differences.

statements.title: Selected skill can jump as computers get cheaper
statements.statement:
Let ${G}$ and ${H}$ be the production functions of the computer and the old-fashioned technology, and ${c}$ the total cost of skill, all functions of the skill level ${s}.$ The pair has *increasing differences in skill* if, whenever ${s\le s'},$
$$H(s')-H(s)\le G(s')-G(s),$$
that is, if ${G-H}$ is non-decreasing.
The cost ${k(t)}$ of the computer technology changes over dates ${t}.$ At each date the firm chooses a technology and a skill level ${s\in S}$ together, earning ${G(s)-c(s)-k(t)}$ with computers and ${H(s)-c(s)}$ with the old technology, and ${\sigma(t)}$ is the largest skill level in an optimal choice. The cost path is admissible if it is continuous and non-increasing, exceeds any given level at some date, and is ${0}$ from some date on. On our first reading of “smoothly”: it is not true that, for all pairs with increasing differences, every cost of skill ${c},$ every set ${S}$ and every admissible cost path ${k},$ the selected skill ${\sigma}$ is continuous in ${t}.$

statements.title: Selected skill can jump even in typical cases
statements.statement:
Let ${G}$ and ${H}$ be the production functions of the computer and the old-fashioned technology, and ${c}$ the total cost of skill, all functions of the skill level ${s}.$ The pair has *increasing differences in skill* if, whenever ${s\le s'},$
$$H(s')-H(s)\le G(s')-G(s),$$
that is, if ${G-H}$ is non-decreasing.
The cost ${k(t)}$ of the computer technology changes over dates ${t}.$ At each date the firm chooses a technology and a skill level ${s\in S}$ together, earning ${G(s)-c(s)-k(t)}$ with computers and ${H(s)-c(s)}$ with the old technology, and ${\sigma(t)}$ is the largest skill level in an optimal choice. The cost path is admissible if it is continuous and non-increasing, exceeds any given level at some date, and is ${0}$ from some date on. On our second reading, “smoothly in the typical case”: it is not true that, for every set ${S}$ of skill levels, there is a dense open set of data ${(G,H,c,k)}$ meeting the conditions above, in the topology of pointwise convergence, at every point of which ${\sigma}$ is continuous in ${t}.$

statements.title: Λ-convex preferences
statements.statement:
Let ${X}$ be a set and ${\Lambda}$ a set of primitive orderings on ${X}.$ A preference relation ${\succsim}$ on ${X},$ complete and transitive, is *${\Lambda}$-convex* if for all ${a,b\in X}$: whenever every ordering ${\ge_\lambda}$ in ${\Lambda}$ admits some ${y_\lambda}$ with
$$b\ge_\lambda y_\lambda\qquad\text{and}\qquad y_\lambda\succsim a,$$
then ${b\succsim a}.$

statements.title: Convexity equals Ψ-convexity for continuous preferences
statements.statement: Let ${X}$ be a convex and closed subset of ${\mathbb{R}^N}.$ Each nonzero vector ${v}$ defines the *algebraic linear ordering* ${x\ge_v y}$ if ${v\cdot x\ge v\cdot y};$ let ${\Psi}$ be the set of all of them. A preference ${\succsim}$ on ${X}$ is *convex* in the standard sense if ${a\succsim b}$ implies ${\alpha a+(1-\alpha)b\succsim b}$ for every ${\alpha\in[0,1]}.$ Then, for a continuous preference ${\succsim}$ on ${X},$ standard convexity is equivalent to ${\Psi}$-convexity in the sense of Definition 1.
statements.conclusion: ${\succsim}$ is convex if and only if it is ${\Psi}$-convex.

statements.title: The textbook’s Λ-convexity implies the paper’s, not conversely
statements.statement:
Let ${X}$ be a set, ${\succsim}$ a preference relation on ${X}$ and ${\Lambda}$ a set of orderings on ${X};$ for ${\trianglerighteq\in\Lambda}$ write ${\triangleright}$ for its strict part. The textbook (Lecture 4) calls ${\succsim}$ *${\Lambda}$-convex* if for every ${y\in X}$ some ${\trianglerighteq\in\Lambda},$ a critical ordering at ${y},$ satisfies
$$\{x: x\succ y\}\subseteq\{x: x\triangleright y\}.$$
The paper’s notion is that of Definition 1. Then:

- (b) a preference that is ${\Lambda}$-convex in the textbook’s sense is ${\Lambda}$-convex in the paper’s sense;
- (a) the converse fails: for some ${X},$ ${\succsim}$ and ${\Lambda},$ the preference is ${\Lambda}$-convex in the paper’s sense but not in the textbook’s.

assumptions.text: For direction (b): ${\succsim}$ is ${\Lambda}$-convex in the textbook’s sense.

statements.conclusion: The textbook’s ${\Lambda}$-convexity implies the paper’s, and the converse implication does not hold in general.
